## 5. Unsafe code

Every unsafe block carries a specific, falsifiable `// SAFETY:` comment: the invariant the
operation relies on, and why it holds on every path that reaches it. Native Rust APIs are
safe unless their caller obligation cannot be expressed in the type system; an `unsafe fn`
documents that obligation in its `# Safety` section.

Unsafe code sits only in a module's unsafe regions and in the raw bindings, as the
[conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section describes. A region that
holds unsafe code of its own takes `unsafe_code` back where it is declared, as
`#[expect(unsafe_code, reason = "<what it reaches>")] mod ffi_import { … }`, so that the
expectation fails once the region holds none; and so does each test suite and unit-test
module that holds unsafe code. A region whose only unsafe code a macro of another crate
expands takes none: the lint does not see that code, and the expectation would fail. A
module with no region carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, which no item within it can take
back.

#!/bin/bash
# run.sh <repo> <package> <cov dir>: build a coverage-instrumented scratch copy of the safe
# crate against the `coverage` variant, its test items under #[coverage(off)], and run each
# suite alone into <cov dir>/prof/<suite>: lib, each integration test binary, and doc. Each
# binary links the variant's C statically, so its profiles count the C and the Rust alike.
# report.py then reads the figures (testing spec, Coverage), with the variant's static archive
# as the C object.
set -euo pipefail
repo=$1 pkg=$2 out=$3
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' "$repo/Cargo.toml")
tree=$out/tree
rm -rf "$out"; mkdir -p "$tree/crustify" "$out/prof"
(cd "$repo" && tar -cf - --exclude=./target --exclude=./crustify --exclude=./c --exclude=./.git .) | (cd "$tree" && tar -xf -)
ln -s "$repo/c" "$tree/c"
ln -s "$repo/crustify/artifacts" "$tree/crustify/artifacts"
ln -s "$repo/crustify/builds" "$tree/crustify/builds"
python3 "$(dirname "$0")/mark.py" "$tree/src" "$tree/src/lib.rs"
cd "$tree"
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=coverage CARGO_TARGET_DIR=$out/target
export RUSTFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage" RUSTDOCFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage -Z unstable-options --persist-doctests $out/doctests"
cargo "+$nightly" test -p "$pkg" --target $host --no-run --message-format=json 2>"$out/build.err" \
  | python3 -c 'import sys,json
for l in sys.stdin:
  try: d=json.loads(l)
  except: continue
  if d.get("reason")=="compiler-artifact" and d.get("executable") and d["target"]["kind"]!=["custom-build"] and d.get("profile",{}).get("test"): print(d["target"]["name"],d["target"]["kind"][0],d["executable"])' > "$out/bins.txt"
cat "$out/bins.txt"
while read -r name kind exe; do
  suite=$([ "$kind" = lib ] && echo lib || echo "$name")
  mkdir -p "$out/prof/$suite"
  echo "== $suite"
  LLVM_PROFILE_FILE="$out/prof/$suite/%p-%m.profraw" "$exe" --skip compile_fail > "$out/$suite.log" 2>&1 || echo "rc=$? in $suite"
  tail -3 "$out/$suite.log"
  "$exe" --list 2>/dev/null | grep -c ': test$' > "$out/$suite.count" || true
done < "$out/bins.txt"
mkdir -p "$out/prof/doc"
echo "== doc"
LLVM_PROFILE_FILE="$out/prof/doc/%p-%m.profraw" cargo "+$nightly" test -p "$pkg" --target $host --doc > "$out/doc.log" 2>&1 || echo "rc=$? in doc"
tail -3 "$out/doc.log"
"""report.py <cov dir> <name>=<dir>[:<dir>...][@<compilation dir>],... --c <C object>...

Merges each suite's profiles under <cov dir>/prof/, the four suites' union as TOTAL and every
suite's as ALL, and prints the TOTAL line of `llvm-cov report` for each named scope, with the C
objects and every test and doctest binary as objects for every suite. A scope's @<dir>
resolves the relative paths a C build recorded. MERGED=1 reuses the merged profiles, and ONLY=<suite> reports that one alone.

A scope written `<name>=@c`, such as `C=@c`, reads the C objects alone, with no source filter:
the archive holds only the link unit's TUs, whatever paths their build recorded. Any other
scope fails when a file it reports lies outside its dirs: llvm-cov falls back to every object
when its filters match no source, which would count the test binaries' std and Rust as C.

The C objects are those of the coverage variant's static archive, its `static` in build.json
(crustify/builds/coverage/crustify/libcrustify.a), which the test binaries link: each binary holds
only the TUs it reaches, so the archive, which llvm-cov reads member by member, gives every TU
its place in the denominator, one no test reaches at zero."""
import subprocess,sys,pathlib,json,glob,os
out0=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
nightly=os.environ.get("NIGHTLY") or next(l.split('"')[1] for l in open(out0/"tree"/"Cargo.toml") if l.startswith("nightly = "))
sysroot=subprocess.run(['rustc','+'+nightly,'--print','sysroot'],capture_output=True,text=True,check=True).stdout.strip()
B=sysroot+'/lib/rustlib/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bin/'
out=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]); scopes=dict(s.split('=',1) for s in sys.argv[2].split(','))
cobjs=sys.argv[sys.argv.index('--c')+1:]
bins=[l.split()[2] for l in (out/'bins.txt').read_text().splitlines()]
docs=[p for p in glob.glob(str(out/'doctests'/'**'/'rust_out'),recursive=True)]
objs=cobjs+bins+docs
suites=sorted(p.name for p in (out/'prof').iterdir() if any(p.glob('*.profraw')))
def merge(name,dirs):
    raws=[str(r) for d in dirs for r in (out/'prof'/d).glob('*.profraw')]
    prof=out/f'{name}.profdata'

---
name: ffimap
description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB, and, as a hint only, when planning an audit's scope and worksets."
---

# ffimap

ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.

It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```

Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \
    --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \
    > <file>.json
```

Raw bindings that are a module of the crate, not a crate of their own, laid out and
generated as [`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes, are named to `--sys-crates`
by their path, `crate::<path>`, beside the `-sys` crates that remain. A named module joins
the inventory and leaves every other counter, as a `-sys` crate does. Left unnamed, its C
types and functions are in no inventory, the cells that read it are taken over the other
crates' alone, and the generated code counts as the crate's own, all with no error. A module
that holds hand-written code beside its declarations is left unnamed, since naming it would
take that code out of the scan.

In a port campaign, a scan names with `--features` the export feature of every module not
yet switched, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Export features section
names them, so that the `ffi_export` gateways compiled under them are counted. Every scan
names the module's unsafe regions, as the conventions' Unsafe regions section names them,
with `--regions`.

Two scans are compared only when they name the same seams, regions and features.

Its counters form one tree, each named by its dotted path into the scan's `counts`, as
ffimap's `docs/schema.md` describes; a metric is a counter, or a combination of counters
that schema allows: a partition's leaves summed, a share read against the record it cuts,
or subtracted from it. `--sites <counter> ...` also lists where each named counter's
increments are, and takes leaves only, such as `fn.unsafe.pub`; the workspace is named
before it. The counters that recur:

- `fn.unsafe.pub`, the public `unsafe fn`s, the crate's public unsafe surface, of which
  `fn.unsafe.of_which.other.pub` are those neither a trait nor a seam required; and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, the raw pointers in
  their signatures;
- `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`, the
  raw pointers in public fields and in the signatures of public safe fns, together
  `raw_ptr.total.safe.pub`, the raw pointers on the safe public interface; and their
  `of_which.void` shares, the type-erased ones among them;
- `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, the references to a cell, less their
  `of_which.self_in_ref_accessor` and `of_which.self_in_trait_impl` shares, the positions
  ffibox sanctions: references to C memory where a handle belongs, which assert `noalias`,
  `readonly` or validity over memory C may write; `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std`, the same
  of the raw C structs; and `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`, the borrows,
  slices and strings formed from a raw pointer, over bytes C must neither free nor change
  while they live;
- `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`,
  each an unchecked assertion that a value may move to or be shared with another thread;
- `raw_ptr.deref.wr` and `raw_ptr.deref.rd`, raw-pointer writes and reads, each a pointer
  the implementer vouches is non-null, aligned, live, initialized and unaliased by a live
  reference; and
- `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}` and
  `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`, the types that hold a raw pointer and
  tear it down or copy it by hand, and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none.{pub,priv}`, those
  that declare nothing about it. Each of these five also has a `.total`, the sum of its two
  leaves, which is no leaf for `--sites`.

ffimap is neither complete nor sound: its sites are where review starts, not all it
covers. It does not count the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, such as a reference
or lifetime-annotated handle made from a raw pointer by `&*p`, `from_ptr`, `from_raw` or
`from_raw_parts`, or changed by a `transmute`: those are found in the source.

What follows is how ffimap serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffimap adds there.

## Binding and porting

### Binding › Safe boundary

Before a batch lands, a scan with `--sites fn.unsafe.pub raw_ptr.field.pub
raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub` lists the public
`unsafe fn`s and the raw pointers on the safe public interface, and each of those sites
that belongs to the batch's changeset and that a safe variant could replace is fixed.
Its `--sites` also name the unsafe code outside both regions,
`code.unsafe_block.of_which.outside_regions`, another crate's macro expansions included,
which the `unsafe_code` lint misses, and `fn.unsafe.of_which.outside_regions.pub` and
`.priv`: outside the raw bindings, each of those sites in the batch's changeset is moved
into its region.

## Accounting

### Accounting › Landing cells

A batch's row in the dashboard's `Batches: safety audit` table is the change in each of
the Safety audit's metrics, from a scan of the tip its landing rebased onto to a scan of
the tree it lands.

### Accounting › API stability

`ffimap api` measures a safe crate's consumer-facing API per C item, from rustdoc JSON, as
its `docs/api.md` describes, read in full before its first use. A C item is the
`<kind>::<path>` of a `Wraps` or `Replaces` anchor, its surface every stand-in the anchor
names and the handles and owners tied to it, each judged by the contract
[`binding-types`](../../rust/binding/types/SKILL.md)' Safe layout section gives a consumer:
the methods every form offers, its reborrows and dereferences, and the traits a consumer
can use, never a form's raw access or seams. A batch generates the safe crate's rustdoc
JSON on the tip its landing rebased onto and on the tree it lands, with a nightly whose
`format_version` the tool supports, and ffibox's, with private items, for the contracts of
the forms it defines:

```bash
cargo +<nightly> rustdoc -p <crate> --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json
ffimap api diff <base>.json <tree>.json --dep <ffibox>.json --items "<the worklist's keys>" --format json
```

Each item comes out `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed` or `new`, with its anchor's
move from `Wraps` to `Replaces` where a port made it. The batch's row in the dashboard's
`Batches: API stability` table counts them over its worklist, and over the crate's
unattributed public items, compared per module.

### Accounting › Records

An unseeded scan of the unsafe and FFI surface is recorded at each batch's, wave's and
the campaign's end, as `ffimap.json` in its artifact directory: a batch's in the run dir
of the run that landed it, a wave's in its wave's dir, as `layout` spells it, and the
campaign's in `crustify/artifacts/`. A module's end is the scan of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

A review locates the sites of its objectives with a scan, `--sites` with their counters,
and keeps those in its workset: the code its commits add or change, or its modules and
the types, trait impls and functions they name. The sites are where the reading starts,
as [`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s Worklists section describes; an
audit's review is the same review with no scan at all.

- `unsafety`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`.
- `contracts`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, whose `# Safety` obligations are evaluated.
- `ub`: these smells first, in this order:
  1. references into C memory: the references to a cell outside its sanctioned positions,
     `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}` less those shares, and to a raw C
     struct, `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, then
     `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`;
  2. thread-safety claims, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and
     `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`, checked against
     the C library's contract: a data race is reachable from safe code when the library
     does not allow what they assert;
  3. the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, found in the source: unsound when the
     handle can outlive the owner of the memory or the point at which C frees or
     invalidates it;
  4. raw pointers a consumer can set, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
     `raw_ptr.field.pub`, with their `of_which.void` shares: unsound when a safe path
     dereferences or frees what the consumer passed or stored;
  5. raw-pointer dereferences, `raw_ptr.deref.wr` then `raw_ptr.deref.rd`: first in the
     modules that also hold references into C memory, where a write may invalidate a
     reference, and outside a type's accessors; and
  6. hand-written teardown and copies, `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}`
     and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`.

## Audit

### Audit workflow › Scope and priority

In an audit a scan is a hint. Where the settings' `tool-hints` answer allows one, it is
run once each build configuration is in place, with `--sites` over the counters of the
audit's objectives, and set beside the reading of the crate: a site the reading missed is
read, and a module the scan reports nothing in is planned and reviewed from its source
like any other. A scan decides neither what is in scope nor its order, and no workset is
dropped, deferred or reviewed more lightly for having no sites.

A scan that fails, that covers part of the crate, such as the files of one configuration,
or that the source contradicts stops nothing: the plan stands on the reading, and the
failure is proposed as ffimap's defect.

### Audit workflow › Worksets

A site of `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop`, `.impl_clone`,
`ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send` or `.sync`, at either leaf, is a trait impl, named
`Drop for <type>`, `Clone for <type>`, `Send for <type>` or `Sync for <type>`. A review
that scans does so over its own modules, so the sites are not passed on.

read, and a module the scan reports nothing in is planned and reviewed from its source
like any other. A scan decides neither what is in scope nor its order, and no workset is
dropped, deferred or reviewed more lightly for having no sites.

A scan that fails, that covers part of the crate, such as the files of one configuration,
or that the source contradicts stops nothing: the plan stands on the reading, and the
failure is proposed as ffimap's defect.

### Audit workflow › Worksets

A site of `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop`, `.impl_clone`,
`ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send` or `.sync`, at either leaf, is a trait impl, named
`Drop for <type>`, `Clone for <type>`, `Send for <type>` or `Sync for <type>`. A review
that scans does so over its own modules, so the sites are not passed on.

#!/bin/bash
# Build the safe crate's Rust static library for a variant's own C to link (crustify's
# porting-workflow skill, Builds): once a module has switched from C, the remaining C, its
# library, CLI and tests, reaches the module through the crate's exports, and its CMake
# build links this library (`LIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY`).
#
#   rust-staticlib.sh <variant> <archive>
#
# Run from the variant's build dir, configured and not yet built, as the first step of its
# `build` command in crustify/artifacts/build.json; <archive> is the library written,
# relative to the build dir, as its configure's `-DLIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY` names it. The crate
# is the one of the checkout this script belongs to, built as a `staticlib` on the dev
# profile, the campaign's tests' own, in campaign mode against this build dir
# (`CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR`) with `CRUSTIFY_STATICLIB` set, so that it reads the build's headers
# and configuration and links none of its C, and with the `bindgen` feature, so that the
# committed bindings are checked against them. Its Rust is instrumented as
# crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh instruments <variant>'s, so that one runtime serves the C
# and the Rust of every C consumer. Cargo's target dir is the build's own, `crustify/cargo`;
# the archive is replaced atomically, so that a link never reads a partial one.
set -euo pipefail
usage='usage: rust-staticlib.sh <variant> <archive>'
variant=${1:?$usage}
archive=${2:?$usage}
[ $# -eq 2 ] || { echo "$usage" >&2; exit 2; }
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
[ -f CMakeCache.txt ] && [ -f build.ninja ] || {
  echo "rust-staticlib.sh: $PWD is not a configured CMake build with the Ninja generator" >&2
  exit 2
}
build=$(pwd -P)
case $archive in /*) ;; *) archive=$build/$archive ;; esac

export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR=$build CRUSTIFY_STATICLIB=1
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=$build/crustify/cargo
crate=(-p libgit2-crustify --lib --locked --features bindgen)
bundled=
case $variant in
  plain)
    out=$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/debug

#!/bin/bash
# Run the target's remaining C tests over a variant's build and compare them with the C test
# baseline (crustify's testing-gates skill, Regressions: a module's switch; setup, Baseline).
#
#   c-tests.sh <variant dir> <out dir> [jobs]
#
# <variant dir> is a built variant, crustify/builds/<variant>, whose C tests link the safe
# crate's Rust static library; its name is the variant whose record of
# crustify/artifacts/c-baseline.json the run is compared with. Nothing is written into it:
# every output goes under <out dir>.
#
# 1. build.json's `test` command, `ctest --output-on-failure -R '^(offline|util)$'`, over a
#    copy of the variant's CTestTestfile.cmake tree, so that ctest's own records stay out of
#    the variant, beside the suites of step 2: <out dir>/ctest.log, its exit status in
#    <out dir>/ctest.rc.
# 2. Every offline libgit2_tests suite and every util_tests suite alone, <jobs> side by side
#    (default 8), each under a 30-minute timeout, as the baseline ran them: TAP output in
#    <out dir>/suites/<binary>/<suite>.{tap,err,rc}. `online::*` suites need the network and

D=crustify/reviews/modules/libgit2/src/util/integer.h/wave-223/batch-1/conventions/static-inline-functions-without-exports && mkdir -p $D && cat > $D/report.md <<'EOF'
class: nit
evidence: reading, against the conventions' Exports section and `porting-symbols`' Static inline functions section; `grep` of the C callers below
conditions: every configuration; `9b43c913d`, the wave's tip before this batch

# integer.h's six `static inline` functions are ported with no export for the C that stays

**Where.** `src/libgit2/src/util/integer_h.rs` as `wave-223/batch-0` landed it (`9b43c913d`).
Its module docs say: "its six `GIT_INLINE` functions and six macros are native Rust here,
reached by no C, so the module has no unsafe regions and no exports". They also say the header stays
"as porting's Macros and Static inline functions sections keep a header's items".

**What is wrong.** `git__is_sizet`, `git__is_ssizet`, `git__is_uint16`, `git__is_uint32`,
`git__is_ulong` and `git__is_int` are `static inline` functions of the module's header. 41
call sites in 20 C files outside the module call them, and most of those files stay past the
first ship point (`posix.c`, `futils.c`, `object.c`, `repository.c`, `odb.c`'s readers of
`pack.c`, `commit_list.c` and others):

```
grep -rn 'git__is_\(sizet\|ssizet\|uint16\|uint32\|ulong\|int\)\b' c/src | grep -v integer.h
```

Three rules say what the module owes those callers:

- The conventions' Exports section: a module's exports are "the module's functions and
  globals that C outside the module references, ..., the `static inline` functions its
  headers define included".
- `porting-symbols`' Static inline functions section: "at the module's switch, the header's
  definition is replaced by its prototype, and the remaining C calls the Rust module's

240 /crustify-rs/crustify.libgit2-crustify/GOALS.md
# Goals

This file states what Crustify is for and how it evolves. Every change to Crustify is judged
against these goals, whether it changes its skills, its agents or its tools.

A rule that serves none of these goals is removed. Where two goals are in tension, they are
weighed for the case at hand, and the weighing is stated.

The goals evolve too, from the same evidence as everything else:

- a goal the campaigns keep missing;
- a goal no decision ever cites;
- two goals that keep conflicting the same way; or
- a well-founded change that none of the goals serves.

A change to the goals is proposed as Crustify's `evolution` skill describes. It lands only
with the user's approval.

Each goal names its *fitness*: what a campaign measures to tell how far the goal is met. Each
thing measured is a *measure*. A measure is read from one of two sources, and no run is made
only to take it:

- what the campaign's runs produce anyway: the dashboard, the review reports, the gates and
  the plan; or
- a rerun the campaign's reviews already make.

A *tier* is one of the checks that code meets one after another. An *escape* is a defect
caught by a later tier than the one that read the code first. Later tiers include:

- a module pass after a wave's review;
- a switch;
- a revisit; and
- a ship point's gates.

Worse work could improve some measures. Such a measure is *paired* with the measure that
catches the worse work, which is its *pair*, and neither is read alone. When there are more
escapes, fewer findings is no gain. When the work is redone, cheaper work is no gain.

Some measures are held by no artifact yet. Such a measure is marked **Not taken yet**. Until
it is taken, what it measures is judged, not measured.

Under each goal, **Measure** states a measure, **Paired with** names its pair, and **Not
taken yet** names what no artifact holds yet.

## 1. Safety

No undefined behaviour is reachable from safe Rust. The unsafe code that remains sits in its
regions, and is sound for every input.

### The unsafe surface

- **Measure.** What a deterministic scan counts on each landing:
  - raw pointers and `unsafe fn`s on the public API;
  - unsafe lines and raw dereferences; and
  - unsafe code outside its regions.

  The first two fall as a module goes from wrapped to ported and through its later stages.
  The third is zero throughout.
- **Paired with** soundness, below. Calling an unsound function safe takes an obligation off
  the API, and so lowers this measure.

### Soundness

- **Measure.** The defects a reproducer proves, as the review reports file them by kind.
  These defects are undefined behaviour and contracts that can be broken.
- **Paired with** the escapes among these defects.
- **Not taken yet.** The tier that caught a defect. Also the unsafe sites a review read,
  which the defects are counted against.

## 2. Equivalence

The Rust keeps the C's specified behaviour, not its bugs. The specified behaviour is what
the C's documentation, tests and consumers rely on.

- **Measure.**
  - The target's own tests passing over the Rust at each switch, against their recorded
    baseline.
  - The inputs and states on which the Rust is compared with the C it replaces, with no
    difference left unexplained.
  - The differences made on purpose, each documented and held by a test.
- **Paired with** the differences found after the comparison ended. They are found by a
  review, at a switch, or by a consumer.
- **Not taken yet.** The inputs compared and the deliberate differences, as figures. Each
  run's notes alone hold them.

## 3. Idiomatic Rust

The API a Rust consumer sees is native Rust: ownership, borrowing, errors, iteration and
traits. It is not C's conventions behind a Rust syntax.

- **Measure.** The C forms that Safety's scan still counts on the public API: raw and
  untyped pointers, and obligations handed to callers. Also the ergonomics and idiom
  findings that reviews file, counted per item reviewed.
- **Paired with** the ergonomics and idiom findings that a later tier or a consumer makes on
  an item an earlier review passed. A review that reads less finds less.
- **Not taken yet.** Which tier made a finding.

## 4. Performance

The emitted Rust costs no more than native Rust would. Where tokens and time buy
accuracy, the harness spends them.

### The harness

- **Measure.** Cost and wall time per translated item, reviews and switches included.
- **Paired with** what was redone: batches run again, gates rerun and merges made twice.
- **Paired with** Safety's and Equivalence's measures: cheaper work with more escapes is not
  cheaper.

### The emitted Rust

- **Measure.** The emitted Rust's time and memory against the C it replaces, on the target's
  own workloads.
- **Paired with** Safety's and Equivalence's measures, since a check dropped is time saved.
- **Not taken yet.** The whole measure.
  <!-- TODO: no campaign benchmarks what it ports; which workloads, and at which event,
  is not specified. -->

## 5. Verification

What the agents produce is machine-checked wherever it can be, rather than left to an
agent's judgement. It is checked by types, lints, sanitizers, Miri, schemas, deterministic
tools and compile-time assertions.

- **Measure.** The line coverage of the ported Rust.
- **Paired with** the share of deliberate faults that the ported Rust's tests catch, since
  code that runs is not code that is checked.
- **Paired with** the gate results that a run reported and that its landed tree does not
  reproduce. A review files these gate results among its reports.
- **Not taken yet.**
  - the seeded faults, which are taken only where a review happens to seed them;
  - the region coverage of the ported Rust; and
  - the states and transitions the tests reach.
  <!-- TODO: seeding faults is not a step of any stage yet. -->

## 6. Maintainability

Established software engineering practice and reuse keep the emitted Rust and the harness
itself maintainable for the long term. Each rule and each piece of code has one place.
Standard libraries and idioms come before new ones.

- **Measure.** What was reused against what was made again:
  - owners, callbacks and lifecycles built from the shared primitives rather than by hand, as
    Safety's scan counts them; and
  - library entities reached through the standard library or an adopted crate rather than a
    new binding, as the plan records each one's route.

  A procedure worked out by hand a second time, and a proposal that repeats another's signal,
  count against this measure.
- **Paired with** Least constraint's measure. Where a rule forces reuse and what is reused
  does not fit, that reuse is counted there.

## 7. Interoperability

C and Rust work together soundly in both directions for as long as both remain. Each reaches
the other through the boundary in its own conventions. The Rust also works with the Rust
ecosystem: the standard library's types and traits, and existing crates where they serve.

- **Measure.**
  - The remaining C's tests passing over the Rust link.
  - The build modes and variants the crate builds and tests in.
  - The kinds of crossing a campaign exercises and passes, in each direction:
    - exports checked against the C declarations they replace;
    - callbacks C makes into Rust and Rust into C; and
    - layouts and storage the remaining C shares.
- **Not taken yet.** The kinds of crossing, as a count.

## 8. Incremental migration without breaking consumers

A codebase moves to Rust one module at a time. Every landing builds and passes its gates. No
consumer breaks: a C or Rust consumer's code does not change as what it consumes is wrapped,
ported or moves through its later stages.

- **Measure.**
  - The items whose API changed or went after their first landing, each with its reason.
  - The landed trees that failed a gate.
  - The target's test baseline, which moves only by the cases carried over.
- **Paired with** Idiomatic Rust's measure of C forms on the public API. An API that never
  changes because it stayed C's breaks no one and serves no one.

### The order

- **Measure.** The batches that met a dependency not yet landed, and waited for it, rewrote
  around it or reached past its wrapper.

  Items land after what they depend on. Where the order cuts a cycle, an item lands after
  the binding of what it depends on. That order is how this goal is met, and Safety's and
  Performance's with it: a consumer written once, over a boundary written once.
- **Not taken yet.** The whole measure.

## 9. Generality

The rules hold for any C codebase. What holds for one target alone is that target's lesson,
not a rule.

- **Measure.** Of what a campaign's evidence taught, the share stated as rules without the
  target's names against the share kept as the target's lessons. Also the rules a second
  target could not follow as written.

## 10. Least constraint

A rule states what must hold. Unless the how is itself what must hold, the rule leaves the
how to the agent.

- **Measure.** Per module, the rules that a run:
  - worked around;
  - rewrote sound code to satisfy; or
  - reported as forcing a worse result.
- **Paired with** what a loosened rule let through: the changes marked as weakening a check,
  and the defects found where a rule was loosened.

## 11. Consistency

One kind of item is translated one way. Items that mean the same in C take the same Rust
pattern, whatever their syntax and whichever agent, batch or campaign translates them. The
pattern is the one the conventions and the how-to skills give them. A departure states its
reason.

A pattern a skill gives is a how that must hold, in Least constraint's terms. A pattern is
given only where translating the same thing two ways costs a consumer or a reviewer. Where
the skills give none, the agent chooses. A choice met twice, where two ways would cost, is
proposed as the pattern rather than left to converge.

- **Measure.** The conventions findings reviews file, per item.
- **Paired with** two measures, since a review that reads less finds less:
  - the items a later batch or review reshaped; and
  - the conventions findings a later tier makes on an item an earlier review passed.
- **Not taken yet.**
  - both paired measures;
  - the departures that state their reason, against the departures a review had to find; and
  - whether an item translated twice took the same shape both times.

## 12. Attribution

Every fact a decision rests on can be reproduced. Every change traces back to the run, and
the revisions, that made it.

- **Measure.** The landed commits, dashboard cells and decisions that trace to a run, its
  session and its revisions, against those that do not. Two examples of those that do not: a
  run without a recorded session, and a figure no rerun of its tool reproduces.

- a well-founded change that none of the goals serves.

A change to the goals is proposed as Crustify's `evolution` skill describes. It lands only
with the user's approval.

Each goal names its *fitness*: what a campaign measures to tell how far the goal is met. Each
thing measured is a *measure*. A measure is read from one of two sources, and no run is made
only to take it:

- what the campaign's runs produce anyway: the dashboard, the review reports, the gates and
  the plan; or
- a rerun the campaign's reviews already make.

A *tier* is one of the checks that code meets one after another. An *escape* is a defect
caught by a later tier than the one that read the code first. Later tiers include:

- a module pass after a wave's review;
- a switch;
- a revisit; and
- a ship point's gates.

Worse work could improve some measures. Such a measure is *paired* with the measure that
catches the worse work, which is its *pair*, and neither is read alone. When there are more
escapes, fewer findings is no gain. When the work is redone, cheaper work is no gain.

Some measures are held by no artifact yet. Such a measure is marked **Not taken yet**. Until
it is taken, what it measures is judged, not measured.

Under each goal, **Measure** states a measure, **Paired with** names its pair, and **Not
taken yet** names what no artifact holds yet.

## 1. Safety

No undefined behaviour is reachable from safe Rust. The unsafe code that remains sits in its
regions, and is sound for every input.

### The unsafe surface

- **Measure.** What a deterministic scan counts on each landing:
  - raw pointers and `unsafe fn`s on the public API;
  - unsafe lines and raw dereferences; and
  - unsafe code outside its regions.

  The first two fall as a module goes from wrapped to ported and through its later stages.
  The third is zero throughout.
- **Paired with** soundness, below. Calling an unsound function safe takes an obligation off
  the API, and so lowers this measure.

### Soundness

- **Measure.** The defects a reproducer proves, as the review reports file them by kind.
  These defects are undefined behaviour and contracts that can be broken.
- **Paired with** the escapes among these defects.
- **Not taken yet.** The tier that caught a defect. Also the unsafe sites a review read,
  which the defects are counted against.

## 2. Equivalence

The Rust keeps the C's specified behaviour, not its bugs. The specified behaviour is what
the C's documentation, tests and consumers rely on.

- **Measure.**
  - The target's own tests passing over the Rust at each switch, against their recorded
    baseline.
  - The inputs and states on which the Rust is compared with the C it replaces, with no
    difference left unexplained.
  - The differences made on purpose, each documented and held by a test.
- **Paired with** the differences found after the comparison ended. They are found by a
  review, at a switch, or by a consumer.
- **Not taken yet.** The inputs compared and the deliberate differences, as figures. Each
  run's notes alone hold them.

## 3. Idiomatic Rust

The API a Rust consumer sees is native Rust: ownership, borrowing, errors, iteration and
traits. It is not C's conventions behind a Rust syntax.

- **Measure.** The C forms that Safety's scan still counts on the public API: raw and
  untyped pointers, and obligations handed to callers. Also the ergonomics and idiom
  findings that reviews file, counted per item reviewed.
- **Paired with** the ergonomics and idiom findings that a later tier or a consumer makes on
  an item an earlier review passed. A review that reads less finds less.
- **Not taken yet.** Which tier made a finding.

## 4. Performance

The emitted Rust costs no more than native Rust would. Where tokens and time buy
accuracy, the harness spends them.

### The harness

- **Measure.** Cost and wall time per translated item, reviews and switches included.
- **Paired with** what was redone: batches run again, gates rerun and merges made twice.
- **Paired with** Safety's and Equivalence's measures: cheaper work with more escapes is not
  cheaper.

### The emitted Rust

- **Measure.** The emitted Rust's time and memory against the C it replaces, on the target's
  own workloads.
- **Paired with** Safety's and Equivalence's measures, since a check dropped is time saved.
- **Not taken yet.** The whole measure.
  <!-- TODO: no campaign benchmarks what it ports; which workloads, and at which event,
  is not specified. -->

## 5. Verification

What the agents produce is machine-checked wherever it can be, rather than left to an
agent's judgement. It is checked by types, lints, sanitizers, Miri, schemas, deterministic
tools and compile-time assertions.

- **Measure.** The line coverage of the ported Rust.
- **Paired with** the share of deliberate faults that the ported Rust's tests catch, since
  code that runs is not code that is checked.
- **Paired with** the gate results that a run reported and that its landed tree does not
  reproduce. A review files these gate results among its reports.
- **Not taken yet.**
  - the seeded faults, which are taken only where a review happens to seed them;
  - the region coverage of the ported Rust; and
  - the states and transitions the tests reach.
  <!-- TODO: seeding faults is not a step of any stage yet. -->

## 6. Maintainability

Established software engineering practice and reuse keep the emitted Rust and the harness
itself maintainable for the long term. Each rule and each piece of code has one place.
Standard libraries and idioms come before new ones.

- **Measure.** What was reused against what was made again:
  - owners, callbacks and lifecycles built from the shared primitives rather than by hand, as
    Safety's scan counts them; and
  - library entities reached through the standard library or an adopted crate rather than a
    new binding, as the plan records each one's route.

  A procedure worked out by hand a second time, and a proposal that repeats another's signal,
  count against this measure.
- **Paired with** Least constraint's measure. Where a rule forces reuse and what is reused
  does not fit, that reuse is counted there.

## 7. Interoperability

C and Rust work together soundly in both directions for as long as both remain. Each reaches
the other through the boundary in its own conventions. The Rust also works with the Rust
ecosystem: the standard library's types and traits, and existing crates where they serve.

- **Measure.**
  - The remaining C's tests passing over the Rust link.
  - The build modes and variants the crate builds and tests in.
  - The kinds of crossing a campaign exercises and passes, in each direction:
    - exports checked against the C declarations they replace;
    - callbacks C makes into Rust and Rust into C; and
    - layouts and storage the remaining C shares.
- **Not taken yet.** The kinds of crossing, as a count.

## 8. Incremental migration without breaking consumers

A codebase moves to Rust one module at a time. Every landing builds and passes its gates. No
consumer breaks: a C or Rust consumer's code does not change as what it consumes is wrapped,
ported or moves through its later stages.

- **Measure.**
  - The items whose API changed or went after their first landing, each with its reason.
  - The landed trees that failed a gate.
  - The target's test baseline, which moves only by the cases carried over.
- **Paired with** Idiomatic Rust's measure of C forms on the public API. An API that never
  changes because it stayed C's breaks no one and serves no one.

### The order

- **Measure.** The batches that met a dependency not yet landed, and waited for it, rewrote
  around it or reached past its wrapper.

  Items land after what they depend on. Where the order cuts a cycle, an item lands after
  the binding of what it depends on. That order is how this goal is met, and Safety's and
  Performance's with it: a consumer written once, over a boundary written once.
- **Not taken yet.** The whole measure.

## 9. Generality

The rules hold for any C codebase. What holds for one target alone is that target's lesson,
not a rule.

- **Measure.** Of what a campaign's evidence taught, the share stated as rules without the
  target's names against the share kept as the target's lessons. Also the rules a second
  target could not follow as written.

## 10. Least constraint

A rule states what must hold. Unless the how is itself what must hold, the rule leaves the
how to the agent.

- **Measure.** Per module, the rules that a run:
  - worked around;
  - rewrote sound code to satisfy; or
  - reported as forcing a worse result.
- **Paired with** what a loosened rule let through: the changes marked as weakening a check,
  and the defects found where a rule was loosened.

## 11. Consistency

One kind of item is translated one way. Items that mean the same in C take the same Rust
pattern, whatever their syntax and whichever agent, batch or campaign translates them. The
pattern is the one the conventions and the how-to skills give them. A departure states its
reason.

A pattern a skill gives is a how that must hold, in Least constraint's terms. A pattern is
given only where translating the same thing two ways costs a consumer or a reviewer. Where
the skills give none, the agent chooses. A choice met twice, where two ways would cost, is
proposed as the pattern rather than left to converge.

- **Measure.** The conventions findings reviews file, per item.
- **Paired with** two measures, since a review that reads less finds less:
  - the items a later batch or review reshaped; and
  - the conventions findings a later tier makes on an item an earlier review passed.
- **Not taken yet.**
  - both paired measures;
  - the departures that state their reason, against the departures a review had to find; and
  - whether an item translated twice took the same shape both times.

## 12. Attribution

Every fact a decision rests on can be reproduced. Every change traces back to the run, and
the revisions, that made it.

- **Measure.** The landed commits, dashboard cells and decisions that trace to a run, its
  session and its revisions, against those that do not. Two examples of those that do not: a
  run without a recorded session, and a figure no rerun of its tool reproduces.

# A header module's `static inline` functions are exported, under a feature named for its header

Status: `open`.

Goal: Consistency. A `static inline` function of a header module is one kind of item with
any other module's, and both take one pattern, an export the remaining C calls after the
switch. Interoperability: the C that stays reaches the module through the boundary.
Fitness: the conventions findings reviews file, per item (Consistency's measure), here six
items of one module.

## Signal

Review findings, and an agent prompt that led its agent wrong. `wave-223/batch-1`, the
module pass of the header module `src/util/integer.h`, filed
`conventions/static-inline-functions-without-exports`. `wave-223/batch-0` ported the header's
six `static inline` functions with no export and no gateway, though C in 19 files calls
them. Its docs cite "porting's Macros and Static inline functions sections" as keeping the
header's items in the header.

## Evidence

- The batch's task message, written for the campaign's first header module with `static
  inline` functions, said "An item the remaining C still expands from the header needs no
  export". The batch read "expands" as covering the functions' bodies, which every caller
  inlines, as well as the macros.
- `porting-symbols`' Static inline functions section says what the switch does with such a
  function: "the header's definition is replaced by its prototype, and the remaining C calls
  the Rust module's export". It does not say that this holds where the module is the header
  alone and the header stays. The Macros section, the one the batch followed, says that a
  header macro "stays in its header for the remaining C, unexported". A header module holds
  both kinds, and the two sections read as one rule.
- The conventions' Export features section names a module's feature `ffi-export-<tu>`,
  "with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root". A header module's
  `translation_unit` is `null` (`modules-schema`), so it has no name to give its feature.
  The review named it for the header, `ffi-export-src-util-integer-h`.
- Earlier header modules (`src/util/strnlen.h`, `deps/ntlmclient/compat.h`) held macros
  alone on this build, so none had met the case.

## Destination

The spec: `porting-symbols`' Static inline functions section, and the conventions' Export
features section.

## Change

In `porting-symbols`' Static inline functions section, after its second sentence, add:

> This holds for a header module too, the header alone, which stays while the remaining C
> includes it: its macros stay in it unexported, as Macros describes, and its `static
> inline` functions are exported, their definitions replaced by prototypes at the switch.

In the conventions' Export features section, after its first sentence, add:

> A header module, which has no translation unit, takes its header's path in its place.

## Validation

Not yet validated. The rerun is the item that exposed it, `wave-223/batch-0`'s six
`fn::git__is_*`, under the change and the same task message. It is expected to write the
gateway under `ffi-export-src-util-integer-h` and to document the header's prototypes, as
`wave-223/batch-1`'s fix did.

## Record

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a header module's `static inline` functions are exported, though the header and its macros stay; a header module's export feature takes its header's path | `libgit2-crustify`, `header-module-exports` | — | a header module's `static inline` functions were ported with no export, read as kept with its macros, and its export feature had no name | a header module whose `static inline` functions the remaining C calls lands with no export, or names its export feature otherwise | — |

## Review

None yet.
EOF

### Reading the batch tables

Batch rows from every sub-campaign share one table per route; the `module` cell names the
row's sub-campaign as `<link-unit>/<module>`, the same name as its Overview row.
Every type row is a `wrap` batch: the rows the wrap campaign landed, kept in the `Types`
tables' `objective` column since the template merged its wrap and port tables. A `wavefront` report category, for ownership findings the review resubmitted, is
counted under `+misc`.

Each batch is measured on two tree states: just before its first landing commit (the wave
base or the previous batch's landing) and its last landing commit. `cov (C/Rust)` is the
latter, from one instrumented build per state: the four workloads (`--lib` unit tests,
`ub_safe`, `ub_unsafe`, `equiv`) each run alone into their own profile directory against
the `coverage` prebuild, and their union is the cell. C is lcov line coverage over the 196
translation units `libgit2.so` links, with a zero baseline from the `.gcno` files so that
untouched TUs count; Rust is cargo-llvm-cov line coverage over `crustify/rust/libgit2`'s
non-`tests/` sources, minus every line inside a `#[cfg(test)]` item (the inline unit-test
modules). All workloads share one denominator, and the union is the union of their covered
lines. Every Rust cell and Rust delta in these tables was restated on 2026-10-12. The
earlier figures counted those test lines, 60% of the instrumented lines at the
`libgit2/index` tip, which held the integration suites' coverage far down and credited
the unit tests for running themselves. All 182 recorded states were re-measured; the C
cells and C deltas stay as first recorded. The eight `libgit2/config` states between
`beeda6a07` and the export revert `c5440d3ee` call the two reverted constructors, so they
were measured against a private coverage build of their own source, which exports them. A Σ `cov` cell is the state after the table's chronologically
last landing. The `(+C/+Rust pp)` pairs in the `…: tests` tables are each workload's own
coverage after minus before, so a batch that adds code its workload does not reach shows a
negative Rust delta. The safety audit deltas are the Safety audit's metrics over the same two
states, from the scans the `ffimap` skill names; the tables hold no row from before the
metrics were redefined, as `Safety audit metrics from ffimap's counter tree` describes.

Test counts are `#[test]` functions the landing commits add, by directory; trybuild
`compile_fail` cases are not counted. `+LoC` and `rv loc` count `.rs` lines under
`crustify/rust/`, so review reproducer crates under `crustify/reviews/` are excluded. The
measurement scripts live outside the repository, beside the orchestrator's other helpers;
each batch's `ffimap.json` beside it is the unseeded scan of its last landing commit.

### Overview test counts

The Coverage stats test lines were measured again on 2026-11-04, at `crustify/devel`
`1e732ebff`, with the testing spec's Coverage method, which replaces the gcov one the
earlier figures used. Those figures are not comparable with these. Each count is the
number of tests its compiled test binary registers (`-- --list`): `--lib` for the unit
tests, one of them ignored, and the `ub_safe`, `ub_unsafe` and `equiv` integration crates.
The trybuild runner is one `ub_safe` test, and it was skipped in the coverage run since it
runs no code. `ub_safe` holds 688 tests since the unsafe fixtures were removed. Doctests
are not counted in the table.

The `coverage` variant, `build.json` version 4, and the side libraries' `coverage`
installs (version 3 of each) compile the C with clang 23,
`-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping`. The Rust is a scratch copy under
`crustify/tmp/coverage/` with `#[coverage(off)]` on every test item, compiled on
`nightly-2026-10-08` (LLVM 23) with `-C instrument-coverage`. Each suite ran alone into
its own profile, and `Total tests` is the merge of the four suites' profiles, their union.
Every figure is the `TOTAL` line of the nightly's `llvm-cov report`, with `libgit2.so` and
every test binary as objects for every suite.

- C is line coverage over the 86,770 lines `libgit2.so` maps to `c/src/libgit2`,
  `c/src/util`, `c/include` and the bundled `c/deps` it compiles (`llhttp`, `ntlmclient`,
  `reftable`, `xdiff`). The generated headers and the C's own tests count toward none.
  libgit2 proper, `src/` and `include/` without `deps/`, is `52.42`% of 68,023 lines. The
  total covers `61.63`% of functions and `47.65`% of regions.
- Rust is line coverage over the 13,226 lines of the crate's 42 files under `src/`, with
  `tests/`, the `-sys` crate and dependencies left out by path. The total covers `99.02`% of
  functions and `97.65`% of regions.
- Doctests, run as a suite of their own: 347, of which 346 pass under the nightly. The
  compile-fail doctest on `CommitBuilder` expects `E0624`, which stable reports and the
  nightly does not; it passes on plain. They reach `11.94`% of C lines and `23.30`% of
  Rust lines, and add no line to the four suites' union.

`crustify/scripts/coverage/` holds the scripts that measured them:
`run.sh "$PWD" libgit2 "$PWD/crustify/tmp/coverage"`, then
`report.py crustify/tmp/coverage "C=$PWD/c/src/libgit2:$PWD/c/src/util:$PWD/c/include:$PWD/c/deps,Rust=$PWD/crustify/tmp/coverage/tree/src" --c crustify/builds/coverage/libgit2.so.1.9.0`.

The UB suites also run under ASan+UBSan, TSan, Miri and BorrowSanitizer in the agents'
gates. Those runs share one test set and are not counted again.

(`try_delta`'s `delta_cache_size`), the ports return nothing; the branches disagree there.

Tests: twelve `unit_pub` tests, which carry over all three cases of `tests/util/integer.c`
(81 products that fit with their values, 63 that overflow, and the four edge cases at this
build's answers, the C case asserting the fallback's) and the inputs of
`tests/util/errors.c`'s `test_errors__integer_overflow_sets_oom`, and check each operation
against `i128` arithmetic over its bounds, the range checks at theirs, and the chain
`patch_parse.c`'s `parse_hunk_body` computes; twelve doctests; and seven `equiv` tests. The
range checks are compared through their raw bindings, the six allowlisted `static inline`
functions `static_fns.c` now wraps (they go with the equivalence tests at the switch), the C's
departures asserted beside the ports' refusals. The macros are compared where they expand:
`git__multiply_sizet_overflow` in `git__calloc`, `git__mallocarray` and `git__reallocarray`;
`git__add_sizet_overflow` in `git_strlist_copy_with_null`; and `git__multiply_int64_overflow`
and `git__add_int64_overflow` in `git_config_parse_int64` and its `git__strntol64`, over signs,
bases and unit suffixes at each bound. `git__add_int_overflow` and `git__sub_int_overflow`
expand only in `parse_hunk_body`, which no raw binding reaches: unreached, checked by the unit
test at its arguments. No C test is tied to the module in `modules.json`; `tests/util/integer.c`
compiles empty on every variant and none of its cases is left uncarried.

Coverage was measured with `crustify/scripts/coverage/run.sh` on a `git archive` of the wave
tip `2d68a9f28` and on this tree, each suite alone, and read with `report.py` from each
scratch tree's `src/libgit2` (`C=@c` over the `coverage` variant's `libcrustify.a`, 88,226
lines; Rust over the scratch tree's `src/`), the unit column merging `lib` and `unit_pub`.
The tip's counts were `equiv` 532 and `unit_pub` 241, where the Coverage stats recorded 538
and 1140 for an earlier tree. The C shifts of suites this batch does not change (`ub_safe`
`+0.01`, `ub_unsafe` `-0.03` pp) and the `equiv` C `-0.02` pp are run-to-run variation.
Worklist: Rust `integer_h.rs` 36 of 36 lines, 36 of 36 regions, 12 of 12 functions; C
`integer.h`'s copies in the archive 4 of 6 functions (`git__is_uint32` and `git__is_ulong`
unreached by any suite, their callers in `diff_tform.c`, `patch_generate.c`, `delta.c` and
`pack-objects.c`), the same as on the tip,
since the wrappers the `equiv` tests call are compiled into the crate, outside the archive.
The Overview's Rust LoC moves by ffimap's `code.loc.total` (`+37`) and `code.tests.loc.total`
(`+632`).

The safety audit scans (ffimap `50a800e`, `--ffibox`, `--sys-crates crate::sys,pcre2_sys`,
the 13 seams, `--regions ffi_import,ffi_export`, no export feature) move only `unsafe loc %`,
by the new safe lines, and the six bindings in `fn.ffibox.sys.total`; the boundary scan's
sites are unchanged, none in the changeset. `ffimap api` against the tip, with ffibox's
private rustdoc JSON (nightly `2026-10-08`): the twelve items are `new`, every unattributed
module `kept` but `sys::libgit2`, `extended` by the six bindings.

## Evidence

`wave-225/batch-0/run-1`, on `git archive 50c93dd23` and on its own tree, after
`crustify/scripts/coverage/run.sh <repo> libgit2-crustify <out>`:

```text
$ python3 crustify/scripts/coverage/report.py <out> "C=@c,Rust=<out>/tree/src" \
    --c crustify/builds/coverage/crustify/libcrustify.a
scope ['<out>/tree/src'] reports 48 files outside it, such as deps/reftable/basics.rs:
its filters match no source
```

`llvm-cov report` prints each file relative to the files' common prefix, here
`<out>/tree/src/libgit2/`, since `src/lib.rs` and `src/sys.rs` hold no counted region.
`report.py`'s stray check resolves each row against its own working directory, so every row
reads as outside the scope, though the filter matched. Run from `<out>/tree/src/libgit2`,
the same command passes and reports the figures the batch recorded.

## Destination

A campaign artifact the assistant owns: `crustify/scripts/coverage/report.py`.

(\`conventions/static-inline-functions-without-exports\`), so that the module's integration
knows what its switch needs and what it gave. Nothing here was committed to \`c/\`.

   prototypes and the macros are left as they are:

   \`\`\`c
$(sed -n '/extern int git__is_/p' $R/integer.h.switched | sed 's/^/   /')
   \`\`\`

   \`integer_h.rs\`'s gateway lost its \`#[cfg(feature = "ffi-export-src-util-integer-h")]\`, as
   the switch deletes the feature.
2. The \`plain\` variant's \`configure\` and \`build\` from \`crustify/artifacts/build.json\`
   (version 7), in a build dir of its own, the side campaigns' installs by absolute path,
   \`rust-staticlib.sh\` run with \`CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE=1\`. The bindings it regenerated
   differ from the committed ones by the six \`#[link_name = "git__is_<name>__extern"]\`
   lines of \`sys/libgit2/bindings.rs\`, and \`sys/libgit2/static_fns.c\` loses its six
   \`git__is_*__extern\` wrappers: the functions are no longer \`static inline\`, so the raw
   bindings reach the exports. The switch commits both.
3. \`nm libgit2.so\` defines \`git__is_int\`, \`git__is_sizet\`, \`git__is_ssizet\`,
   \`git__is_uint16\`, \`git__is_uint32\` and \`git__is_ulong\` as local text symbols from the
   Rust library, and no \`*__extern\` wrapper.
4. \`crustify/scripts/c-tests.sh\` over that build: \`3442\` passed, \`0\` failed, \`55\` skipped
   of \`3497\`, no non-zero suite, which matches the baseline's \`plain\` record; \`ctest\`
   exited 0. A first run, with \`c/\` a \`git archive\` and no \`.git\`, failed
   \`perf::merge::m1\` and skipped \`blame::simple::trivial_libgit2\` and its cache-pressure
   twin: they open the checkout at \`tests/resources/../..\` as a repository.

The other variants were not built, and neither was the packaging gate.
EOF

361 /crustify-rs/ffimap/docs/api.md 670 /crustify-rs/ffimap/docs/schema.md 1031 total 50a800e scanner: the revision is ffimap's own checkout's, and names its uncommitted changes # API stability per C item `ffimap api` measures a promise a C-to-Rust migration makes to its Rust consumers: once a C item has a safe Rust API, wrapping it, porting it and its later stages leave that API alone. It reads the crate's rustdoc JSON, finds the Rust items that stand in for each C item through their anchors, and records their consumer-facing surface twice: raw, as the signatures stand, and as the **contract** a consumer may rely on whatever form a handle or an owner takes. Two such records, one at the item's first landing and one after a later landing, say whether the contract was kept, extended or changed. This document is what the two documents hold and every rule behind them. The scan's counters are [`schema.md`](schema.md)'s and have nothing to do with it. ## 1. Input ```sh cargo +nightly-2026-10-07 rustdoc -p CRATE --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json (cd ffibox && cargo +nightly-2026-10-07 rustdoc --lib -- -Z unstable-options \ --output-format json --document-private-items) ffimap api extract target/doc/CRATE.json --dep ffibox/target/doc/ffibox.json > before.json ``` `--dep` gives the rustdoc JSON of a crate the measured one depends on, and is repeatable. The contracts of handles and owners that are aliases into ffibox (`CBox`, `CArc`, `CVal`, …) need ffibox's, since the reborrows and trait impls those forms inherit live there; it is made with `--document-private-items` because the bounds rustdoc synthesises for ffibox's auto-trait impls name its private fields' types. Without it those contracts are unresolved, as section 6 describes. The measure is pure Python over the JSON. It does not use the driver, so the crate need not build on the driver's nightly, only document on one whose JSON format it reads. Rustdoc's JSON is unstable: each nightly writes a `format_version`, and the shape moves with it. `ffimap api` reads **format 61**, which nightly-2026-10-07 (the driver's pin) and nightly-2026-10-08 emit, and refuses any other with an error naming the version it found. Support for a new format is added by checking the fields `src/ffimap/rustdoc.py` reads against it and adding it to `FORMAT_VERSIONS`. ## 2. C items and their stand-ins A C item is keyed by its anchor's `::`: `fn::git_mailmap_new`, `st::git_mailmap`, `fld::git_buf.ptr`. An anchor is a doc-comment line of its own, exactly ``Wraps `::` `` or ``Replaces `::` ``, where the path is names separated by dots and a `fld` path names a member. Every public item of the crate that carries one is a **stand-in** of that C item, and an item carrying several (the accessor of two members) is a stand-in of each. What the extract reports about the anchors themselves, under `anchors`: - `malformed`: a line that tries to be an anchor and is not one -- the verb and a `kind::` path inside a sentence, with a trailing period, without backticks, or with a path that is not names. It keys nothing. - `unknown_kinds`: anchors whose kind is not one of the convention's (`fn`, `st`, `un`, `enm`, `fnp`, `tdf`, `fld`, `glb`, `mac`), counted by kind. They are keyed as written. - `without_alias`: anchors on an item with no `#[doc(alias)]` naming the anchor's path. An item whose own name is the anchor's path is left out: rustdoc rejects an alias equal to its item's name, and the name already answers a search for it. ## 3. Locators and paths Each stand-in is named by a **locator**, which is how one landing's record is matched with the next's: | item | locator | |---|---| | a free item | its canonical path | | an item of an inherent impl | `Ty::name` | | an item of a trait impl | `>::name` | | a trait's item, a variant, a field | its owner's locator `::name` | Lifetime names in a locator are erased to `'_`. A **canonical path** is the path a consumer names an item by. For an item of the crate it is the path rustdoc's `paths` table gives its definition when that path is public, else the shortest public path it is re-exported at, the first in order among equals. An item defined in a private module and re-exported from its parent is named by the parent's path, and a port that moves the definition into the parent changes nothing. An item of another crate is named by its definition's path in the `paths` table, `ffibox::refs::CBox` for instance, because this document does not record that crate's re-exports. Every type in a signature is rendered by its canonical path, never by what the source wrote, so an import or a reordering of the source gives the same bytes. A record's `paths` lists every public path the item is reached by, from the crate root through public modules and `pub use`, globs included. An associated item's are its owner's paths with its name appended. ## 4. Signatures Each stand-in's `sig` is normalised text by kind: - **functions and methods**: `decl` holds `const`, `async`, `unsafe`, the ABI, generics, the receiver (`self`, `&self`, `&'a mut self`, `self: Box`), the parameter types and return type, and where-clauses. A method also has the `impl` header it is declared in, generics and trait included, and a trait's method has `default`, whether it has a body. Parameter names are left out. - **structs, enums and unions**: `decl` holds the generics, the shape (`;`, `(n)`, `{}`) and `#[non_exhaustive]`. `fields` maps each public field to its type, and `variants` each variant to its shape and discriminant. `stripped` says whether rustdoc hid private fields or variants. `impls` maps the header of every trait impl rustdoc records for the type to its items (those it defines and the trait's provided ones it inherits) and its associated types and constants; the auto-trait impls rustdoc synthesises (`Send`, `Sync`, `Unpin`, `UnwindSafe`, `RefUnwindSafe`, and `Freeze` and `UnsafeUnpin` where the nightly records them), negative ones as `!Send`, are included, and blanket impls are not, since they follow from the type's other impls. `members` holds the items of its inherent impls that stand in for no C item, each with its impl header. - **traits**: `decl` with generics, supertraits and `unsafe`; `required` and `provided` items, each with its declaration; `dyn_compatible`. - **type aliases**: `decl` holds the whole target, `type = ffibox::refs::CBox<…>`. - **constants and statics**: type and value; **associated constants and types**: their declaration and, in an impl, its header; **variants** and **fields**: their shape or type; a `macro_rules!` macro only its kind, since its body is not an interface. A trait impl's methods are recorded by name only: their signatures are the trait's, recorded where the trait is. ## 5. Handles and owners The types a consumer reaches a C type through -- `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooBox`, `FooArc`, `FooVal` and a policy type such as `FooFree` -- are not always annotated. An unannotated public struct, enum, union or trait of the crate is **associated** with C items by rule 1, else by rule 2, and a type alias by rule 3; `via` says which rule tied it: 1. `assoc_type`: a trait impl of the type sets an associated type to an anchored type, or a trait impl of an anchored type sets one to it. `impl CRefSeam for MailmapRef { type Cell = Mailmap; }` and `impl CCell for Mailmap { type Ref<'a> = MailmapRef<'a>; }` both tie `MailmapRef` to `st::git_mailmap`. 2. `owner`: the type's impls, or the trait's declaration, hold stand-ins; it is associated with their C items. A policy type whose `CDrop::c_drop` wraps `fn::git_mailmap_free` goes with that item. 3. `alias`: a type alias whose target names an anchored type, by id anywhere in the target, goes with that type's C items: `MailmapBox = CBox` with `st::git_mailmap`. A target naming none goes with the items of the types it names that rules 1 and 2 associated. An associated item is recorded under each of its C items with the record a stand-in has, and a C item's surface is its stand-ins and its associated items together. ## 6. The contract view A handle or an owner changes form over a migration: `FooRef` is a pointer wrapper while `Foo` is wrapped and `&'a Foo` once it is ported, `FooBox` an ffibox `CBox` and then a `Box`. A consumer relies only on what every form offers, as `binding-types` states: their methods, their reborrows (`as_ref`, `as_mut`) and the dereferences the native forms offer. What the measure cannot see - **What no anchor reaches.** An unannotated type that no rule of section 5 ties to an anchored one is attributed to its module, not to a C item. - **The route to a method.** A contract flattens methods over dereferences and reborrows, so a method callable directly on one form and only through `as_ref()` on another reads the same. - **Lifetimes in contracts.** They are erased, so a getter returning a borrow of the handle and one returning a borrow of its target read the same. - **Standard types beyond the model.** A form that is an `Option`, a `Vec` or any standard type other than the pointer forms is unresolved, and so is a bound on a generic alias's free parameter. - **Behaviour.** A signature that stays while what the function does changes reads as kept. - **Renamed generics.** Generic parameter names are kept in declarations, so renaming `T` or a lifetime reads as changed, except in locators, where lifetimes are erased. - **Another crate's re-exports.** A dependency that moves a definition behind an unchanged re-export renders differently, since this document has only the definition's path. - **Semver nuance.** A change is anything lost or rewritten, whether or not a consumer could tell: a bound loosened or a where-clause reordered reads as changed. A contract's impl bounds are checked against impl lists only, one impl at a time, with no inference beyond what rustdoc recorded. - **Trait-impl method signatures.** They are the trait's; a change to an unanchored, unattributed trait is reported under its module only. - **Hidden items.** Rustdoc leaves `#[doc(hidden)]` items and private ones out of its JSON, so neither they nor anchors on them are seen.

content.content:
## Safety audit

Deterministic `ffimap`, run as the `ffimap` skill's Accounting section describes; no
model. Every counter is in the `ffimap.json` tracked in the campaign's artifact dir, in
each wave's `waves/wave-<index>/` and in each batch run's dir. Each metric is one counter
or a combination of counters, named by their dotted paths into the scan's `counts`; a `%`
metric is a share within one record, and a `−` subtracts a share from the record it cuts.

### Metrics

| metric | counters | what it counts |
|---|---|---|
| pub raw ptr | `raw_ptr.total.safe.pub` | raw pointers a consumer meets without writing `unsafe`: public fields and the signatures of safe public fns; target 0 |
| pub void ptr | `raw_ptr.field.of_which.void.pub` + `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.of_which.void.{safe,unsafe}.pub` + `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.of_which.void.{safe,unsafe}.pub` | type-erased pointers left to the API's users, `unsafe fn`s included |
| pub unsafe fn | `fn.unsafe.pub` | the obligations the crate exports to its callers |
| &cell | `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.pub` − `….of_which.self_in_ref_accessor.pub` − `….of_which.self_in_trait_impl.pub` | public references to a cell outside the positions ffibox sanctions, where the convention wants a handle; target 0 |
| C by value | `ty.ffibox.sys.as.by_val.total` + `ty.ffibox.sys.as.owned.std.total` | C structs held by value or in a standard-library owner rather than through a cell, which a move can leave dangling |
| celled % | `ty.ffibox.sys.of_which.raw_ptr_in_sys.of_which.wrapped` / `….of_which.used` | of the C types the bindings pass by pointer that the crate uses, those a cell covers |
| raw→std | `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.total` | raw pointers turned into a standard-library borrow, slice, string or owner, whose lifetime or ownership the type system then trusts |
| unmanaged ptr types | `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none.total` | types that store a raw pointer and declare nothing about it |
| ptr Drop | `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.total` | types that store a raw pointer and free it by hand, rather than through an owner |
| Send/Sync | `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.total` + `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.total` | thread safety asserted rather than derived from the fields |
| raw deref | `raw_ptr.deref.total` | raw-pointer reads and writes in bodies, each a pointer the code vouches for |
| FFI calls | `code.unsafe_call.ffi` | calls across the C boundary, through bindings or stored function pointers |
| unsafe loc % | `code.loc.unsafe` / `code.loc.total` | lines of unsafe code over code lines; the comparable measure of unsafe volume |
| unsafe blocks | `code.unsafe_block.total` − `code.unsafe_block.of_which.ffi_export` | hand-written unsafe blocks, a port's generated export gateways left out; moves with the one-op-per-block policy, so not comparable across crates |

import json,sys
def g(c,path):
    cur=c
    for p in path.split('.'):
        cur=cur[p]
    return cur
def m(f):
    c=json.load(open(f))['counts']
    G=lambda p:g(c,p)
    r={}
    r['pub raw ptr']=G('raw_ptr.total.safe.pub')
    r['pub void ptr']=G('raw_ptr.field.of_which.void.pub')+G('raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.of_which.void.safe.pub')+G('raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.of_which.void.unsafe.pub')+G('raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.of_which.void.safe.pub')+G('raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.of_which.void.unsafe.pub')
    r['pub unsafe fn']=G('fn.unsafe.pub')
    w='ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std'
    r['&cell']=G(w+'.pub')-G(w+'.of_which.self_in_ref_accessor.pub')-G(w+'.of_which.self_in_trait_impl.pub')
    r['C by value']=G('ty.ffibox.sys.as.by_val.total')+G('ty.ffibox.sys.as.owned.std.total')
    r['celled %']=100*G('ty.ffibox.sys.of_which.raw_ptr_in_sys.of_which.wrapped')/G('ty.ffibox.sys.of_which.raw_ptr_in_sys.of_which.used')
    r['raw→std']=G('raw_ptr.casted_to.std.total')
    r['unmanaged ptr types']=G('ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none.total')
    r['ptr Drop']=G('ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.total')
    r['Send/Sync']=G('ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.total')+G('ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.total')
    r['raw deref']=G('raw_ptr.deref.total')
    r['FFI calls']=G('code.unsafe_call.ffi')
    r['unsafe loc %']=100*G('code.loc.unsafe')/G('code.loc.total')
    r['unsafe blocks']=G('code.unsafe_block.total')-G('code.unsafe_block.of_which.ffi_export')
    r['_loc']=G('code.loc.total'); r['_tests_loc']=G('code.tests.loc.total'); r['_loc_unsafe']=G('code.loc.unsafe')
    return r
a=m(sys.argv[1])

A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.

An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
way.

## 3. Worktrees

Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.

## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
